explanation: Bei regelmäßigen Verben bildet man das Simple Past mit der Endung -ed: "play -> played", "walk -> walked", "jump -> jumped". Endet das Verb schon auf -e, hängt man nur -d an: "love -> loved".
options: Add -ing to the verb (play -> playing, walk -> walking)
Add -s to the verb (play -> plays, walk -> walks)
Add -ed to the verb (play -> played, walk -> walked)
Add -es to the verb (go -> goes, watch -> watches)
question: How do you form the Simple Past of regular verbs?

explanation: "Go" ist ein unregelmäßiges Verb: go -> went -> gone. Die Simple-Past-Form ist "went": "I went to school yesterday." Die dritte Form "gone" braucht man dagegen für das Present Perfect: "I have gone."
options: goed
went
gone
goes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "go"?

explanation: "Write" ist ein unregelmäßiges Verb: write -> wrote -> written. Die Simple-Past-Form ist "wrote": "She wrote a letter yesterday." Nach have/has steht dagegen die dritte Form: "She has written..."
options: writed
wrote
written
wrotes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "write"?

explanation: "Take" ist ein unregelmäßiges Verb: take -> took -> taken. Im Simple Past heißt es "took": "He took the book yesterday." Die dritte Form "taken" gehört zum Present Perfect.
options: taked
tooken
took
taken
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "take"?

explanation: Das Present Progressive (Verlaufsform) bildet man mit am/is/are + Verb + -ing: "I am reading.", "She is watching TV.", "They are playing." Man benutzt es für Handlungen, die gerade jetzt ablaufen, und für vorübergehende Situationen.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (I will read)
Subject + have + past participle (I have read)
Subject + am/is/are + verb + -ing (I am reading)
Subject + verb + -s (She reads a book)
question: How do you form the Present Progressive (Verlaufsform)?

explanation: Das Present Progressive steht 1) für das, was gerade jetzt passiert: "I am eating." 2) für Vorübergehendes: "She is living in London for a year." 3) für feste Pläne in der nahen Zukunft: "We are meeting tomorrow."
options: For permanent facts and general truths (Water freezes at 0 degrees)
For actions happening around now (I am studying this week)
For finished past events at a named time (We visited Rome in 2019)
For plans that are still uncertain (Maybe I will travel)
question: When do we use the Present Progressive?

explanation: Das Simple Present benutzt man für Gewohnheiten ("I usually get up at 7.") und für Tatsachen ("The earth orbits the sun."). Das Present Progressive beschreibt, was gerade jetzt passiert ("She is calling you.") oder was nur vorübergehend gilt ("He is working in Paris this month.").
options: There is no real difference; both tenses can always be exchanged
Simple Present: habits and facts. Progressive: happening now
Simple Present is the politer form and is used in formal speech
The Progressive is used in writing only, the Simple Present in speech
question: What is the difference between Simple Present and Present Progressive?

explanation: Fragen im Simple Past bildet man mit did + Subjekt + Grundform des Verbs (kein -ed!): "Did you go to school?", "Did she write the letter?" Falsch ist "Did you went?", denn did zeigt die Vergangenheit schon an.
options: Verb + subject + ? (Went you to school yesterday?)
Did + subject + infinitive? (Did you see the film yesterday?)
Have + subject + past participle? (Have you gone there?)
Will + subject + infinitive? (Will you go there?)
question: How do you form a question in Simple Past?

explanation: Verneinungen im Simple Past bildet man mit didn't + Grundform, nicht mit der Vergangenheitsform: "I didn't see him." (nicht "I didn't saw him"), "She didn't go." (nicht "She didn't went").
options: Subject + no + past tense verb (I no saw him)
Subject + didn't + infinitive (I didn't see him)
Subject + not + past tense verb (I not saw him yesterday)
Subject + wasn't + infinitive (I wasn't go)
question: How do you form a negative in Simple Past?

explanation: Present Perfect (have/has + Partizip II): 1) Erfahrungen: "I have been to Paris." 2) Ergebnis der Vergangenheit relevant jetzt: "She has lost her key." 3) Mit yet, already, just, ever, never.
options: Only for finished actions at a named past time (last Tuesday, in 1990)
For experiences and results that matter now (She has just arrived)
Only for future events that are already planned (next week, tomorrow)
For habits that happen again and again (every day, on Mondays)
question: What is the Present Perfect used for?

explanation: Present Perfect: have/has + Partizip II (3. Form). "I have eaten." "She has gone." "They have played." Das Partizip II regelmäßiger Verben endet auf -ed, unregelmäßige muss man lernen: go/went/gone, see/saw/seen.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (She will go to school)
Subject + have/has + 3rd form (I have eaten)
Subject + am/is/are + -ing (She is going home now)
Subject + did + infinitive (She did go yesterday)
question: How do you form the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Used to" + infinitive: früherer Zustand/Gewohnheit, die jetzt nicht mehr gilt. "I used to eat meat but now I am vegetarian." Nur in der Vergangenheit!
options: A future habit that will be repeated regularly (I will go every day)
A past habit or state that no longer exists (I used to play piano, but not any more)
A present habit that happens regularly and has not changed (I play piano)
A polite request directed at someone else (Could you help me?)
question: What does "used to" express?

explanation: Mit dem Komparativ (der ersten Steigerungsstufe) vergleicht man zwei Dinge. Kurze Adjektive bekommen die Endung -er: "tall -> taller". Lange Adjektive stehen mit more: "beautiful -> more beautiful". Das Wort "than" bedeutet "als".
options: To say that something is the highest in a group (the superlative)
To compare two things (She is taller than her brother)
To describe a noun more exactly (a very big house)
To ask about qualities (How tall is he?)
question: What are comparative adjectives used for?

explanation: "Good" wird unregelmäßig gesteigert: good -> better -> best. Deshalb heißt es "This book is better than that one." Weitere unregelmäßige Steigerungen: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, many/more/most, little/less/least.
options: gooder
more good
better
goodest
question: How do you form the comparative of "good"?

explanation: Lange Adjektive mit drei oder mehr Silben bilden den Superlativ (die höchste Stufe) mit most: "most interesting", "most beautiful". Kurze Adjektive bekommen dagegen die Endung -est: "big -> biggest".
options: interestinger
most interesting
interestingest
more interesting
question: How do you form the superlative of "interesting"?

explanation: Das "going to"-Futur bildet man mit am/is/are + going to + Grundform: "I am going to visit Paris next year." Man benutzt es für Pläne und Absichten oder wenn man jetzt schon sieht, dass etwas passieren wird.
options: Subject + going to + past tense verb (I going to walked home yesterday)
Subject + am/is/are + going to + infinitive (I am going to travel)
Subject + will + going + infinitive (I will going visit Paris next year)
Subject + to + going + infinitive (I to going visit Rome)
question: How do you express the future with "going to"?

explanation: "I will help you!" (spontane Entscheidung). "I am going to visit Rome next summer." (Plan steht schon fest). Beides ist Zukunft, aber mit unterschiedlicher Bedeutung.
options: There is no difference at all; both forms can always be exchanged freely
Will: spontaneous decisions or predictions. Going to: fixed plans
Will is only used in written English, going to only in spoken English
Going to describes past plans, while will describes present intentions
question: What is the difference between "will" and "going to"?

explanation: Conditional I (reale Bedingung): If + Simple Present, will + infinitive. "If the weather is nice, we will go swimming." Reale/mögliche Bedingung.
options: If + Simple Past, would + infinitive (If it rained, I would stay)
If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If it rains, we will stay at home)
If + Past Perfect, would have + past participle (If it had rained, I would have stayed)
If + will + infinitive, will + infinitive (If it will rain, I will stay)
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 1 (real condition)?

explanation: Conditional II (irreale Bedingung): If + Simple Past, would + infinitive. "If I were rich, I would help everyone." Irreale/unwahrscheinliche Bedingung.
options: If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If I have money, I will travel)
If + Simple Past, would + infinitive (If I had a million euros, I would travel the world)
If + Present Perfect, would have + past participle (If I have saved, I would travel)
If + Future, will + infinitive (If I will have money, I will travel)
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 2 (unreal condition)?

explanation: Ein Relativsatz gibt zusätzliche Auskunft über ein Nomen: "The girl who lives next door is my friend." Dabei gilt: who = für Personen, which = für Dinge, that = für beides, where = für den Ort, when = für die Zeit.
options: A clause that says when something happens, using when or while (when I was young)
A clause that adds information about a noun (The book that I read was good)
A clause that describes an unreal situation with if (If I were rich, I would travel)
A clause that gives a purpose (so that she could win)
question: What is a relative clause?

explanation: "Who" = für Personen. "The man who called is my uncle." "The girl who wrote the letter." Für Sachen benutzt man dagegen which oder that.
options: For things and objects (The book who I read was interesting)
For people (The teacher who taught us)
For places (The city who I visited last summer)
For times (The day who we met was sunny)
question: When do we use "who" in a relative clause?

explanation: Im Passiv steht eine Form von be + Partizip II (dritte Verbform): "The letter was written by her." Also am/is/are/was/were + Partizip II. Das Aktiv betont, wer etwas tut, das Passiv das Ergebnis.
options: She wrote a long letter to her aunt.
The letter was written by her.
She is writing a letter to her friend.
She had written the letter last week.
question: Which sentence uses the passive voice?

explanation: Das Passiv im Simple Present bildet man mit am/is/are + Partizip II: "English is spoken here.", "Milk is sold in shops.", "Books are printed in factories."
options: Subject + have been + past participle (have been built)
Subject + is/are + being + past participle (is being built)
Subject + am/is/are + past participle (is built, are sold)
Subject + will + past participle (It will built)
question: How do you form the passive in Simple Present?

explanation: Modalverben (modal verbs) drücken Fähigkeit, Erlaubnis oder Pflicht aus: can (können), could (könnte), must (muss), should (sollte), may (darf), might (könnte), will (wird), would (würde). Sie bekommen in der 3. Person Einzahl kein -s, und danach steht immer die Grundform.
options: Regular verbs that follow the normal rules (play -> plays -> played)
Auxiliary verbs for ability, permission or obligation (can, must, should, may, might)
Irregular verbs whose past forms must be learnt by heart (go -> went -> gone)
Verbs that always end in -ing and describe ongoing actions (running, eating)
question: What are modal verbs?

explanation: "Must" = interne Notwendigkeit/Regel. "I must study" (ich fühle die Pflicht). "Have to" = externe Notwendigkeit. "I have to wear a uniform" (Schule schreibt es vor). Oft kann man beide Formen benutzen.
options: Must and have to always mean different things and can never be exchanged
Must: personal obligation. Have to: obligation from outside.
Must is the past tense form of have to and describes past obligations
Have to is always more polite and more formal than must
question: How do you express obligation with "must" vs "have to"?

explanation: "Should" = sollte, Empfehlung. "You should see a doctor." "He shouldn't eat so much sugar." Es ist schwächer als "must" und gibt einen Rat, keine strenge Vorschrift.
options: Certainty - something will definitely happen (It will rain tomorrow)
Advice or a recommendation (You should eat more fruit)
Obligation - a strict rule you must follow (You must wear a helmet)
Permission - giving someone the right to do something (You may go now)
question: What does "should" express?

explanation: Englische Fragen brauchen ein Hilfsverb vor dem Subjekt. 1) Bei be, have oder can tauschen Subjekt und Hilfsverb einfach die Plätze: "Is she happy?" 2) Im Simple Present und Simple Past steht do/does/did + Subjekt + Grundform: "Do you know her?"
options: Just add a question mark to a statement (You like pizza?)
Use do/does/did or an auxiliary before the subject (Do you like pizza?)
Put the main verb at the very end, as in German (You pizza like?)
Always start with the subject and then the verb, as in a statement (You like pizza?)
question: How do you form questions in English?

explanation: Question tags sind kurze Rückfragen am Satzende. Nach einem bejahten Satz steht der verneinte Anhang: "It's cold, isn't it?" Nach einem verneinten Satz steht der bejahte Anhang: "You don't know, do you?"
options: Very long questions that ask for a lot of information (Where did you go?)
Short questions added to a statement to confirm it (It's nice, isn't it? / You can swim, can't you?)
Questions that begin with why and ask for a reason (Why are you late?)
Questions that begin with how and ask about the manner (How did you do that?)
question: What are tag questions?

explanation: "Neither...nor" heißt "weder...noch": Beides trifft nicht zu. "I have neither a pen nor a pencil." Zum Vergleich: "either...or" heißt "entweder...oder".
options: An alternative choice - one of two options is possible (either ... or)
Two negatives - not the one and not the other (Neither he nor she)
Both possibilities - two things are true at the same time (both ... and)
A limitation - only one single thing is allowed (only ...)
question: What does "neither...nor" express?

explanation: In der indirekten Rede gibt man wieder, was jemand gesagt hat: "He said he was tired." (direkt: "I am tired.") Die Zeitform rückt dabei einen Schritt zurück: am -> was, will -> would, can -> could. Mit "that" kann man beide Satzteile verbinden.
options: Direct speech - repeating the exact words in quotation marks (I am tired)
Indirect speech - telling what someone said (He said he was tired)
A question that asks someone to repeat what they just said (Sorry?)
A command that tells someone to do something at once (Close the door!)
question: What is reported speech?

explanation: Richtig ist "I agree with you." Falsch sind "I am agree" und "I am agreed", denn "agree" ist ein Zustandsverb. Solche Verben (agree, know, understand, believe, like, love) stehen normalerweise nicht in der Verlaufsform mit -ing.
options: I am agree with you
I agree with you
I am agreeing with you
I am agreed with you
question: Which sentence is correct?

explanation: Zustandsverben (state verbs) beschreiben einen Zustand, keine Handlung, und stehen deshalb nicht in der Verlaufsform: "I know" (nicht "I am knowing"), "I like" (nicht "I am liking"), "She owns a car" (nicht "she is owning").
options: Action verbs that describe movement or activity (run, jump, swim, dance)
Verbs that describe a state, not an action, and take no -ing form (know, like, own)
Irregular verbs whose past tense and past participle must be learnt by heart (go, went, gone)
Modal verbs that express ability or obligation (can, must, should, may)
question: What are "stative verbs" (Zustandsverben)?

explanation: "As well as" = sowohl...als auch / sowie. "She can sing as well as dance." "He likes history as well as geography." Es fügt eine zusätzliche Information hinzu.
options: aber / however - introducing a contrast to what was just said (but, however)
sowie / ebenfalls - adding extra information (She plays piano as well as guitar)
weder ... noch - saying that neither of two things is true (neither, nor)
entweder ... oder - presenting two alternatives to choose from (either, or)
question: What does "as well as" mean?

explanation: "Although/Even though" = obwohl. "Although she was tired, she continued working." "Even though it was expensive, he bought it." Es leitet einen Gegensatz ein: Etwas spricht dagegen, trotzdem passiert es.
options: To give a reason for something that happened (because, since, as)
To express a contrast (Although it was raining, we went outside)
To describe the result of a previous action (so, therefore, that is why)
To express a time relationship (when, while, before, after)
question: How do you use "although/even though"?

explanation: "Unless" = es sei denn / wenn nicht. "I'll help you unless you are rude." = "I'll help you if you are NOT rude." Nach "unless" steht also eine bejahte Bedingung, gemeint ist aber die Verneinung.
options: wenn / if - introducing a simple condition (If it rains, I will stay at home)
es sei denn dass / wenn nicht (I will come unless it rains tomorrow)
weil / because - giving a reason (because it was late)
obwohl / although - introducing a contrast (although it was late)
question: What does "unless" mean?

explanation: Häufigkeitsadverbien (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) stehen vor dem Hauptverb: "I often read." Nach einer Form von "be" stehen sie dagegen dahinter: "She is always tired."
options: Always at the very end of the sentence, after the object (I read books often)
Usually before the main verb, but after be (She is always late)
Always at the very beginning, before the subject (Often I read books)
Only in questions, never in normal statements (Do you often read?)
question: How are adverbs of frequency used?

explanation: "Much" steht vor unzählbaren Nomen: "much water, much time, much money". "Many" steht vor zählbaren Nomen in der Mehrzahl: "many books, many people, many hours". In bejahten Sätzen sagt man oft einfach "a lot of".
options: There is no difference; both words work with every kind of noun (much books)
Much: for uncountable nouns. Many: for countable nouns (much water, many books)
Much is the polite form, many is used in everyday speech (many time)
Many is used only in questions, much only in statements (How many water?)
question: What is the difference between "much" and "many"?

explanation: "A few" = ein paar (zählbar): "a few books, a few friends." "A little" = ein wenig (unzählbar): "a little water, a little time." Beide klingen leicht positiv: Etwas ist da, wenn auch nicht viel.
options: There is no difference; both words mean the same (a few water, a little books)
A few: a small number (countable). A little: a small amount (uncountable)
A few is negative and means that almost nothing at all is left (a few money)
A little means none at all (a little water = no water)
question: What is the difference between "a few" and "a little"?

explanation: Gerund: Verb + -ing als Nomen. "Swimming is my hobby." (Subjekt). "She enjoys reading." (Objekt nach enjoy, like, love, hate, avoid, finish, suggest). Auch nach Präpositionen steht das Gerund.
options: Verb + -ed, so that the past tense form is used as a noun (played is my hobby)
Verb + -ing, used as a subject or an object (Swimming is fun)
Verb + -s, the third person form used as a noun (plays)
Verb + -tion, making a noun from a verb (information)
question: How do you form the gerund (-ing form used as noun)?

explanation: Verben die Gerund verlangen: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, imagine, miss, practise, consider. "I enjoy swimming." "She avoids eating sugar." "Do you mind waiting?" bedeutet: Stört es dich zu warten?
options: After to, want and would like (I want to swim / I would like to go home)
After enjoy, avoid, finish, mind (I enjoy swimming / She avoids sugar)
After will, would, can and must (modals are followed by the bare infinitive)
After hope, decide, promise (I hope to win / She decided to leave)
question: After which verbs do we usually use a gerund (-ing)?

explanation: "Whereas" = wohingegen, während hingegen. Drückt einen Kontrast aus. "Some people are morning persons, whereas others prefer evenings." Ähnlich: while, in contrast to.
options: weil / because - giving the reason for something that happened (because it rained)
wohingegen / während - expressing a contrast (She likes tea, he likes coffee)
obwohl / although - showing something unexpected (although it was cold)
damit / so that - expressing a purpose (so that she could win)
question: What does "whereas" mean?

explanation: "So...that" = so...dass. Es nennt die Folge einer Eigenschaft: "It was so heavy that I couldn't lift it." "She was so tired that she fell asleep immediately."
options: To show a contrast between two different or opposite situations
To show a result or consequence
To show the reason or cause that explains why something happened
To show a condition that must be met for something to happen
question: How do you use "so...that"?

explanation: Simple Present: 1) Gewohnheiten: "I play football on Sundays." 2) Allgemeine Wahrheiten: "The sun rises in the east." 3) Fahrpläne/Programme: "The train leaves at 8."
options: Actions happening at this very moment while you speak (I am eating now)
Habits, routines and general truths (Water boils at 100 degrees)
Completed past events at a fixed point in time (I went home)
Plans already decided for later (I am flying to Rome)
question: What does the Simple Present express?

explanation: In der 3. Person Einzahl (he/she/it) hängt man -s an: "play -> plays". Endet das Verb auf s, x, ch, sh oder o, kommt -es dazu: "watch -> watches", "go -> goes". Unregelmäßig ist "have -> has".
options: No change at all - the verb keeps its base form (he play, she watch)
Add -s or -es (he plays, she watches, it goes)
Add -ing to the base form (he playing, she watching, it going)
Add -ed to the verb (he played, she watched)
question: How do you form the Simple Present for he/she/it?

explanation: Fragen im Simple Present bildet man mit do (bei I/you/we/they) oder does (bei he/she/it) + Subjekt + Grundform: "Do you know her?", "Does he live here?" Nach "does" bekommt das Verb kein -s mehr.
options: Verb + subject? (Likes she pizza? Plays he chess?)
Do/Does + subject + infinitive? (Do you like pizza? Does she play chess?)
Did + subject + infinitive? (Did you like pizza?)
Will + subject + infinitive? (Will you like pizza?)
question: How do you form Simple Present questions?

explanation: Simple Past: abgeschlossene Handlungen in der Vergangenheit, oft mit Zeitangabe: yesterday, last week, in 1999, ago. "I visited Berlin last summer."
options: Ongoing past actions that were still in progress at a given moment
Completed actions in the past at a specific time
Present habits that repeat regularly in everyday life
Future intentions or plans that have already been arranged
question: What is the Simple Past used for?

explanation: "Just" + Present Perfect: etwas ist gerade eben passiert. "He has just called you." "I have just finished my homework." Es steht zwischen have/has und dem Partizip II.
options: That something happened a very long time ago, in the distant past
That something happened very recently, only a moment ago
That an action will happen at a future point
That an action was repeated many times
question: What does "just" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Already" = schon/bereits. "I have already done my homework." Es sagt, dass etwas früher passiert ist als erwartet, und steht meist zwischen have/has und dem Partizip II. Man benutzt es vor allem in bejahten Sätzen.
options: That something has not yet happened but is expected to happen soon
That something happened sooner than expected
That something will definitely happen at some point in the future
That something happened long ago
question: What does "already" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Yet" = noch nicht (negativ) / schon (Frage). "I haven't done my homework yet." "Have you called her yet?" Es steht am Satzende.
options: That something has already been done sooner than expected
That an expected thing has NOT happened yet, or asking whether it has
That something will be done at a later point
That an action was done over and over again
question: What does "yet" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Ever" = jemals (in Fragen): "Have you ever eaten sushi?" "Never" = nie: "I have never seen snow." Beide Wörter beziehen sich auf Erfahrungen im ganzen bisherigen Leben.
options: Specific times in the past when something happened or did not happen
Experience at any time in your life, or at no time
Plans and intentions for the future that may still change
Regular present habits and routines that happen at fixed times
question: What do "ever" and "never" indicate with Present Perfect?

explanation: Past Progressive: was/were + -ing. Beschreibt laufende Handlung zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt in der Vergangenheit. "At 8pm, she was cooking dinner." Oft kommt ein Simple Past dazu, wenn etwas diese laufende Handlung unterbricht.
options: A past action that was fully completed at one named point in time
An action in progress at a certain moment in the past
A habit repeated regularly in the past
An action completed before another past action
question: What is the Past Progressive (Verlaufsform der Vergangenheit)?

explanation: Das Past Progressive bildet man mit was (bei I/he/she/it) oder were (bei you/we/they) + Verb + -ing: "I was sleeping.", "They were playing football."
options: had + past participle (I had gone, they had eaten)
was/were + verb + -ing (I was sleeping)
did + verb + -ing (I did going, they did eating)
used to + infinitive (I used to go)
question: How do you form the Past Progressive?

explanation: Kombination: "While I was walking home, it started to rain." Past Progressive = laufende Hintergrundhandlung. Simple Past = kurze Unterbrechung.
options: The two tenses are never used together in one and the same sentence
Past Progressive gives the ongoing background action, Simple Past the shorter event that interrupts it
Past Progressive always comes after Simple Past to show what happened next
Simple Past describes the ongoing background, Past Progressive the interruption
question: How is the Past Progressive used with the Simple Past?

explanation: Past Perfect: had + Partizip II. Vorvergangenheit. "When I arrived, she had already left." Ereignis 1 (she left) geschah BEVOR Ereignis 2 (I arrived). Signalwörter: after, before, when, by the time.
options: Another name for the Simple Past, used for ordinary past events
had + past participle, for an earlier past action
was/were + -ing, an action in progress at a past moment
used to + infinitive, a habit that no longer exists today
question: What is the Past Perfect?

explanation: Richtig ist "By the time she arrived, we had already eaten.", denn das Past Perfect braucht had + Partizip II (eaten). "By the time" heißt "bis zu dem Zeitpunkt, als..." und steht meist mit dem Past Perfect.
options: After I had went to the station, I bought a ticket.
By the time she arrived, we had already eaten.
She had eat the cake before the guests came.
They had been go home when the film started at eight.
question: Which sentence uses the Past Perfect correctly?

explanation: "Will" Future: 1) Spontane Entscheidungen: "I will answer that!" 2) Vorhersagen: "It will be sunny." 3) Versprechen: "I will always love you." 4) Angebote: "I will carry that for you."
options: Fixed plans and arrangements that have already been decided in advance
Spontaneous decisions, predictions, offers and promises
Past habits and routines
States that exist at the present moment
question: What does the Future with "will" express?

explanation: "Going to": Plan schon festgelegt: "I am going to visit my aunt on Sunday." Voraussage mit Beweis: "Look! He's going to fall!" Unterschied zu will: Spontan vs. geplant.
options: They are always interchangeable
For plans that were already made, and for predictions based on evidence you can see right now
Going to is more polite and is therefore preferred in formal situations
Will is for fixed plans, going to for spontaneous decisions
question: When do we use "going to" instead of "will"?

explanation: Simple Past Signalwörter: yesterday, last (week/month/year), ago, in [year], when I was (a child), once, at that time.
options: already, just, ever, never, yet, so far, up to now
yesterday, last week, in 2010, three days ago
tomorrow, next week, soon, in a few days, later
now, at the moment, currently, right this second
question: Which time expressions are typically used with the Simple Past?

explanation: Present Perfect Signalwörter: already, just, yet, ever, never, recently, lately, so far, this (week/month/year), since, for.
options: yesterday, last year, in 2010, three months ago, at that time, once
already, just, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, this year
tomorrow, next week, next month, in two years
now, at the moment, right now, currently, at this very second
question: Which time expressions are typically used with the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Since" + Zeitpunkt: "since 2010, since Monday, since she left." Es nennt also den Startpunkt und steht mit dem Present Perfect: "I have known her since we were children." Für die Dauer benutzt man dagegen "for".
options: A duration of time with the Simple Past, as in since three years
A point in time, used with the Present Perfect
A duration with the Simple Present
A specific date with the Simple Past
question: What is "since" used with?

explanation: "For" + Zeitdauer: "for two hours, for a week, for ten years." Mit dem Present Perfect: "I have lived here for five years." Es ist aber auch im Simple Past möglich: "She worked there for a year."
options: A specific point in time, such as a weekday
A length of time, that is how long something lasts or has lasted
The beginning of an action
A date in the calendar
question: What is "for" used for in time expressions?

explanation: Erzählerische Vergangenheit: Simple Past. "Once upon a time, there was a princess. She lived in a castle. One day, a knight arrived..." Past Progressive für Hintergrundbeschreibungen.
options: Simple Present, describing all the events as if they happened right now
Simple Past, sometimes with Past Progressive
Present Perfect, linking the past events to the present moment
Future with will, predicting how the events will unfold
question: What tense do we use to tell a story (narrative tense)?

explanation: Future Progressive: will be + -ing. Zukünftige Handlung im Verlauf zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt. "This time tomorrow, I will be flying to London." Betont den Verlauf.
options: Going to + -ing (I am going to reading all evening)
Will + be + -ing (I will be studying)
Was/were + -ing (I was studying all evening)
Had + been + -ing (I had been ill)
question: What is the future progressive?

explanation: Fahrpläne/Programme/Spielpläne: Simple Present. "The bus leaves at 9:15." "School starts on Monday." "The film finishes at 10pm." Feste Zeiten im Kalender.
options: Will + infinitive (The train will leave at eight tomorrow morning)
Simple Present (The train leaves at eight)
Going to (The train is going to leave)
Simple Past (The train left)
question: How do we express a scheduled/timetabled future event?

explanation: Simple Past: abgeschlossen, spez. Zeitpunkt. "I saw her yesterday." Present Perfect: Verbindung zur Gegenwart, kein spez. Zeitpunkt. "I have seen her." (Leben, Ergebnis jetzt wichtig).
options: There is no real difference, both simply describe events in the past
Simple Past means finished at a definite time in the past, Present Perfect links the past to now without naming a time
Simple Past is formed with have or has plus the past participle
Present Perfect uses did plus the infinitive in questions
question: What is the main difference between Simple Past and Present Perfect?

explanation: "How long have you + Past Participle?" fragt nach der Dauer einer Handlung, die begann und noch läuft. "How long have you known her?" "I have known her for 3 years." Antwort: for/since.
options: A single past event that happened once at a definite moment
How long an action has been going on
A future plan that has already been decided and arranged
An action that was finished before another past event
question: What does "How long have you...?" ask about?

explanation: Nach Zeitkonjunktionen (when, before, after, until, as soon as) steht für die Zukunft das Simple Present! "When she comes, we will eat." NICHT "When she will come".
options: Present Progressive (I will call you when I am arriving there)
Simple Present (I will call you when I arrive)
Future with will (I will call you when I will get there)
Simple Past (I called you when I arrived)
question: What tense do we usually use after time conjunctions like "when, before, after, until" for future?

explanation: Past Perfect mit after/before: zeigt Reihenfolge. "After he had eaten, he went to bed." (essen kam zuerst). "Before I arrived, she had already left." Hatte schon getan.
options: It is never used with these words, another tense is always needed
It shows which of two past events happened first
It describes a future action
It describes a regular past habit
question: What is the Past Perfect used for with "after" and "before"?

explanation: Nach einem Modalverb steht die Grundform des Verbs ohne "to": can swim, must go, should eat. Falsch sind deshalb "can swimming", "must goes" oder "should to go".
options: The past form with -ed (can played, must walked, should talked)
The infinitive without "to" (can swim, must go, should eat, may come)
The -ing form (can swimming, must going, should eating)
The past participle (can swum, must gone)
question: Which verb form follows a modal verb?

explanation: "Could" = könnte/konnte. 1) Fähigkeit in der Vergangenheit: "When I was young, I could run fast." 2) Höfliche Bitte: "Could you help me?" 3) Möglichkeit: "It could rain."
options: can (I can swim when I was five / Can you help me?)
could (I could swim when I was five / Could you help me?)
must (I must swim when I was five / Must you help me?)
will (I will swim when I was five / Will you help me now?)
question: How do you say "könnte" (past ability/polite) in English?

explanation: "Must not/Mustn't": verboten. "You mustn't run here." "Don't have to/Doesn't have to": nicht nötig. "You don't have to wear a tie." Völlig verschiedene Bedeutung!
options: There is no difference at all, the two expressions mean exactly the same
Must not = forbidden, don't have to = not necessary
Must not means that something is optional and you may choose freely
Have to is never used in questions, only must can be used there
question: What is the difference between "must" and "have to" in questions/negatives?

explanation: "Might" = könnte, vielleicht. Schwache Möglichkeit. "I might go to the party." Unsicherer als "may". "It might snow tomorrow."
options: Certainty - that something will definitely happen without any doubt
Possibility - that something may or may not happen
Obligation - something you must do because of a rule or a duty
Ability - being capable of doing something
question: What does "might" express?

explanation: "Will" für Versprechen und Schwüre: "I will always be there for you." "I will never forget you." Spontane Entscheidung/Versprechen -> will.
options: I am going to loving you forever.
I will always be there for you.
I have always loved you.
I was loving you at that time.
question: Which sentence is in the correct future form for a promise?

explanation: "Was/were about to" = wollte gerade... "I was about to call you when you called me." Drückt aus, dass eine Handlung kurz vor der Ausführung war, als etwas anderes geschah.
options: I had already finished something before something else happened
I was just going to do something when something else happened
I usually did something as part of my daily routine
I wanted to do something but decided against it
question: What does "I was about to..." mean?

explanation: Present Perfect + since: "She has worked here since 2018." Die Handlung begann 2018 und dauert bis jetzt an. Möglich ist auch das Present Perfect Progressive, das die Dauer betont: "She has been working here since 2018."
options: Since + Simple Past (Since I worked here two years, I know everyone)
Have/has + past participle + since + a point in time (I have lived here since 2010)
Since + Present Progressive (I am living here since 2010)
Since + will future (I will live here since 2010)
question: How do you form the Present Perfect with "since" to show duration?

explanation: "Used to": vergangene Zustände UND Gewohnheiten. "I used to live in Berlin." (Zustand) "Would": nur vergangene Gewohnheiten. "Every Sunday, he would cook a big meal." NICHT "I would live in Berlin."
options: Both are used only for present habits that happen regularly today
Used to also covers past states, would only past actions
Used to describes plans for the future, would describes completed past actions
Would is used for regular present habits, used to for single past events
question: What does "used to + infinitive" vs "would + infinitive" describe?

explanation: Historisches Präsens: Vergangenes im Präsens erzählen, um Lebhaftigkeit zu erzeugen. "So I go to the shop, and suddenly I see him!" Gesprochene Sprache, lebhafte Erzählung.
options: The use of present tense only in fictional novels and short stories
Telling past events in the present tense to make them more vivid
The normal and most common way of telling any kind of story in English
A special future tense for predicting events in a story
question: What is the "narrative present"?

explanation: Zeitungsschlagzeilen: Simple Present für abgeschlossene Ereignisse. "Man Finds Treasure in Garden." "Fire Destroys Hotel." Das Präsens macht Schlagzeilen kurz und dynamisch.
options: Actions going on right now while the newspaper is being read
Past events shown in the present for a dramatic effect
Future plans that are scheduled to happen soon
Situations that may or may not occur
question: What does the "present simple" express in headlines?

explanation: Future Perfect: will + have + Partizip II. "By next year, I will have lived here for 10 years." Handlung wird vor einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt in der Zukunft abgeschlossen sein.
options: Will + be + -ing (I will be finishing school by 2025)
Will + have + past participle, for actions finished before a future point in time
Would + have + past participle, the conditional perfect
Am going to + past participle (I am going to finished)
question: What is the Future Perfect?

explanation: "Hardly/scarcely/barely...when": kaum...als. Bei Voranstellung folgt Inversion: "Hardly had I arrived when it started raining." = "I had hardly arrived when it started raining."
options: A time clause saying that two events both happen regularly
One thing happened immediately after another
A condition where one event causes the other to happen
A contrast between two events at very different times
question: What does "hardly/scarcely/barely...when/before" express?

explanation: "By the time you read this, I will have already left." Future Perfect für eine Handlung, die VOR einem Zeitpunkt in der Zukunft abgeschlossen sein wird.
options: will have left (Future Perfect)
had left (Past Perfect)
have left (Present Perfect)
will leave (Will Future)
question: Which tense is correct in: "By the time you read this, I ___ already ___."?

explanation: Eine Form von be + Partizip II ergibt immer das Passiv. Im Simple Present: "English is spoken worldwide." Im Simple Past: "The letter was written." Im Present Perfect: "The bridge has been built."
options: Active voice in the present (Many people read this book)
The passive voice (The book is read by many people)
The progressive form (Many people are reading the book)
The perfect form (Many people have read the book)
question: What is "to be + past participle" in terms of tense/voice?
